As for the ordering of the headers, HPACK itself is not required to preserve ordering of the header fields.
Actually, it is permitted to reorder the input header set before encoding. The output is inherently out of order because of reference set. The consensus of the ordering issue is that the relative ordering of the header field sharing the same header name may matter. If the application want to preserve its relative ordering, the application has to concatenate those header values into single header field in the manner described in http://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-http2-09#section-8.1.3.3

The same header set means they were generated from the same har file.
I think story_XY.json files sharing same number (XY) must have the same header fields, otherwise something is broken.
If you insist on which, I'd like to say it is in raw-data directory.

Specifically, story_26.json and story_31.json were generated from https://github.com/http2/http_samples/blob/master/mnot/facebook.com.har.
If you dump header fields and sort them from those files and compare them, you will see they contain exactly same header fields.
The difference is, other than the lack of 'seqno' in story_26.json, the order of header fields.
The problem I wrote in the last comment is that story_31.json just causes corner case for particular encoder implementation (nghttp2 in this case).  This is because whether the corner case appears or not depends on how implementation processes header fields.  For example, corner case may disappear if  header fields are sorted before encoding. This means that this new story is not effective to other implementations and does not cause corner cases at all.
This also means that we cannot create HPACK test cases in our json format to cover certain corner case for encoder.  On the other hand, our test cases are quite effective for decoder implementations.
